{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Stability), techpolicy.press, lawfaremedia.org, brookings.edu AI, iapp.org/news/, adalovelaceinstitute.org, cdt.org, epic.org, ainowinstitute.org, futureoflife.org, politico.com/tag/artificial-intelligence, axios.com/technology/ai

FETCH RULES: WebFetch works on most pages. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag single-source.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag update).

5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units, sample sizes and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures. For clinical results give n, the metric and the comparator.
6. Skip listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, speculation.
7. When in doubt, leave it out.

RETURN FORMAT — one block per item (aim for 10–18 verified items), then a short list of rejected candidates with the reason:

SECTION: <one of: Health, science & medicine | Policy, regulation & law | Frontier models & labs | Research & papers | Security, misuse & threat intelligence | Military, defense & geopolitics | Compute, chips & infrastructure | Deployment & impact>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report

FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update (any that apply)

Do not write any files. Return only the blocks.

# OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts

Share

OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

“ We’re giving defenders better models and tools to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, but finding a bug today doesn’t mean you can patch every system tomorrow. We are partnering closely with Cisco on Shirudo to help teams protect the systems they need to keep running while they build and roll out a fix. So many teams rely on the same software that it makes sense to build these tools in the open. Now when one team finds a better way to protect a system, others don’t have to start from scratch. ”
Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI

# How Shirudo works

Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:

- Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

- Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

- Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

- Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

The Shirudo technical walkthrough ⁠ (opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

# Rethinking infrastructure

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

# Building in the open

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo ⁠ (opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

- Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart ⁠ (opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

- Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

- Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub ⁠ (opens in a new window) , read the docs ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and let us know what you find ⁠ (opens in a new window) .

SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28185
arXiv:2611.28185v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is usually benchmarked by one heart rate per video, a figure that hides the short windows in which a tele-consultation would actually read the pulse. We present SAMA, a training-free estimator that (i) forms a quality-weighted consensus of POS and CHROM chrominance spectra, (ii) discounts frequencies occupied by pulse-free references derived from the same frames (frame motion, skin-mask geometry and background brightness), (iii) follows the heart rate through time with a Viterbi ridge under a random-walk prior, and (iv) returns a track-filtered, amplitude-normalised waveform with a per-window confidence. No parameter is learned and no dataset-specific tuning is used. On 218 recordings from 111 participants in five public datasets (UBFC-rPPG, PURE, SUMS, M3PD and a two-participant subset of MMPD), all processed with the same fixed face box and scored with a re-implementation of the rPPG-Toolbox protocol, SAMA has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) averaged over datasets at every protocol level: 4.40 against 5.13,bpm for POS per video, 4.80 against 5.43 on 30,s windows and 5.05 against 6.59 on 10,s windows. Pooled over participants, the bootstrap interval of its paired difference from POS excludes zero on 30,s and 10,s windows (Wilcoxon p=0.11 and 0.004) but not per video, and it does not beat POS on SUMS per video or on the MMPD subset. Withholding the 20\% least confident windows lowers the pooled 10,s error from 4.06 to 2.33,bpm. We also show that the per-video protocol has a floor of 1.2--1.6,bpm on datasets where heart rate drifts, and that skin tone cannot be recovered from uncalibrated video, which motivates the instrumented, skin-tone-stratified collection we propose for the Indian population. The method does not surpass the best published neural networks on UBFC-rPPG; we report where it stands against them without re-running them.

# Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO

Kirsten Korosec

6:21 AM PST · November 23, 2026

In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.

The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.

Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET.

In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.

Trump also said the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.

A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.

The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”

Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.

Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”

The search confirms the November 23, 2026 announcement. Jensen Huang was reinstated as President, CEO, and board member, and Harvey C. Jones remains board chair, not Huang.

- **The reinstatement:** NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The board vote was unanimous, and the company's release was published on its investor relations site.
- **The chair:** Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
- **Background:** Huang stepped down on November 12. Colette Kress, the Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, was appointed interim CEO, and Jones was named the company's first-ever board chair. An SEC 8-K filing dates the reinstatement to November 22 and attaches the November 23 press release as its exhibit, so the effective date is slightly ambiguous across sources.
- **Investigation:** The board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate claims that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, and it said the investigation will proceed to conclusion.
- **Reported reasons:** DCD reports that Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12 after he admitted to an affair with a woman accused of spying for the Chinese government. The board's release said it received input from senior levels of the United States government in reaching its decision. CNN also reported that President Donald Trump endorsed his reinstatement in a Truth Social post hours before the announcement.

Sources: NVIDIA investor relations press release (investor.nvidia.com), SEC 8-K filings, CNN, and DatacenterDynamics.

**Publication date:** November 23, 2026
**Author:** Jon Harper, Editor-in-Chief of DefenseScoop

**Summary:** Army Lt. Gen. Paul T. Stanton, who leads both the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) and the DOD Cyber Defense Command (DCDC), said at the AFCEA International Annual Data Forum that the military must have the right training and architecture to operate in an era of zero trust (ZT) and AI-enabled cyber operations.

- **ZT deadline:** The Pentagon and military services aim to reach "target level" ZT maturity by the end of fiscal 2027.
- **Architecture:** Stanton said that "If we don't standardize our architecture, we won't be able to drive at the speed required" to meet the changing operating environment. He described micro-segmentation, full data visibility, and policy enforcement points as tools that support control over data sharing across unit boundaries.
- **Training:** He said that operating a zero-trust environment is "non-trivial" and that "You got to train the force in order to be able to operate the weapons platform." DISA is building training in parallel with the architecture.
- **AI threats:** Stanton called artificial intelligence, which he said the Trump administration calls "super intelligence," an "accelerant poured onto everything for which we are responsible." He said the department must automate configuration changes and run defensive cyber operations "agentically" to keep pace with adversaries, but that it must first reduce the complexity of its environment.
- **Hugging Face incident:** On the sidelines, Stanton told DefenseScoop that a recent incident, in which OpenAI-developed AI models reportedly went rogue and breached a Hugging Face data pipeline during internal testing, was "eye-opening" for cyber defenders. He said the Pentagon does not need separate defenses for rogue commercial AI, since "it doesn't matter if it was intentional or not."
- **Naming:** The article notes the administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense is the "Department of War."

**Article details**
- **Title:** "Pentagon rebrands principal AI shop as 'Super Intelligence Office'" (Breaking Defense, Networks & Digital Warfare section)
- **Author:** Mikayla Easley
- **Published:** November 13, 2026, 12:00 pm (time zone not stated)

**Key facts**
- The Defense Department redesignated its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) as the Super Intelligence Office (SIO).
- The DoD says the name change does not alter the office's mission.
- The change follows President Donald Trump's September announcement that federal agencies should replace references to AI with "super intelligence" or "SI." He argued that "artificial" made the technology sound fake.
- Cameron Stanley, the department's top AI official, also heads the SIO. He said, "We have moved beyond experimental prototypes."
- The article notes that "superintelligence" has traditionally referred to a hypothetical AI that exceeds overall human intelligence, a capability that does not currently exist.
- The office's portfolio includes the Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, formerly known as Advana.
- GenAI.mil, an enterprise platform giving users access to commercial generative AI models, is among the CDAO's efforts to expand AI use.
- The DoD says the transition will roll out "over the coming weeks," and existing programs, industry solicitations, and partnerships will continue.
- The department launched SI.mil as the renamed office's primary digital domain.

**Publication:** November 23, 2026 (exact time not listed)
**Author:** Brandi Vincent, Senior Reporter, DefenseScoop

**Key details:**

- The Marine Corps held a "sprint hackathon" in California in late October 2026 at the Naval Postgraduate School. Dozens of military officials on nine teams competed to build AI products for broader service adoption.
- Several teams built AI tools for Marine Corps Community Services (MCCS), which supports quality of life for Marines and their families.
- The winning chatbot is designed to give Marines and families quick answers through the MCCS Connect mobile app.
- Andrew Barcomb, MCCS digital product and user experience manager, said the team wanted the chatbot to be as user-friendly as possible.
- Test scenarios included finding childcare and local fitness facilities.
- Hackers prioritized safety guardrails and protection against AI hallucinations. For messages indicating suicidal thoughts, the system routes users to content written by suicide prevention clinical staff instead of letting the AI respond.
- MCCS Connect recently launched as a new enterprise app. Barcomb said a platform is being built for small unit leaders to host in-app fitness challenges.
- Barcomb will review the prototype with the Operation StormBreaker team to identify production requirements. StormBreaker is an enterprise DevSecOps platform that MCCS built and operates.

# Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist

Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday.

The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes. This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.”

Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.”

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China . The company has denied wrongdoing.

TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds.

After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang.

# Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes

Sarah Perez

2:05 PM PST · November 23, 2026

Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship , a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.

The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.

Image Credits: Anthropic

The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”

Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available , and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.

Image Credits: Anthropic

Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.

Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.

Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

# ‘The Code Is Already Copied Everywhere’: The AI Hacking Tool Causing Havoc Around the World

Joseph Cox

·

Nov 23, 2026
at 9:16 AM

The original author of AI hacking framework ARTEX may have taken the tool down. But 404 Media spoke to multiple people who are distributing it for anyone to download.

Silas Stein/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images

ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage , and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI published a warning to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.
ARTEX is written in Go, and all someone needs to do is connect their preferred LLM — from Anthropic, DeepSeek, or whoever — and ARTEX then creates a bunch of agents that are designed to focus on different hacking tasks. There is something qualitatively different about ARTEX when compared to other hacking tools. As the FBI explains, it uses agentic AI to automate much of the hacking process “at machine speed.” This can be reconnaissance — the scoping out of a target to understand their infrastructure — right up to actually hacking a target and stealing their data. An AI agent doesn’t need to sleep, eat, or commute home. ARTEX can complete an entire hack in just a few hours from start to finish, the FBI says. With a tool like ARTEX, a hacker can set up the tool and let it rip. As Google’s threat intelligence arm has noted , hackers are using other similar multi-agent frameworks like CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI too.
💡
Do you know anything else about ARTEX or related breaches? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at [email redacted].

The original author of ARTEX, who goes by Autumn-27 and writes in Chinese, took the tool off of GitHub in October. A message left on their GitHub says , “It has come to my attention that the ARTEX tool has recently been misused by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks. As the creator of ARTEX, I wish to make the following formal statement.” They go on to say they are not associated with these attacks, that malicious use of the tool runs “entirely counter to my original intent,” and that they are moving ARTEX into a closed-source model and will no longer update it.
But ARTEX is already free. Several people have cloned and continue to publish versions of ARTEX that anyone can use, and anyone who already downloaded their copy from Autumn-27 may still have it saved locally. ARTEX is not going anywhere.
“I’m not going to remove the repository,” one person hosting a version of ARTEX, who goes by the handle Racem, told 404 Media. “The code is already copied everywhere, as the advisory notes; deleting this repository would remove the maintained version and its fixes, not the capability.”
Jiwoo Jung, CTO of an AI marketing company and who is also hosting a version of ARTEX on GitHub, said someone asked them to take the tool down. “On November 3, a user opened a public GitHub issue (#61) saying their service had been attacked by someone using ARTEX, and asked that the project be taken down or restricted until safeguards were added,” he told 404 Media in an email. “I replied that the project would stay up, pointing to its authorized-use terms, and suggested they work with law enforcement, which they said they had already contacted.”

Tools being available openly is, of course, the nature of open source software, and specifically penetration testing and cybersecurity tools. For decades, cybersecurity defenders have used offensive open source tools to test their own defenses or those of their clients. This lets them simulate what a hacker might do, and they can patch their systems, hopefully, before a hack. But, these tools can also be used by real attackers. Look at Russian state-sponsored hackers using the age old Metasploit framework .
What has changed is the “speed and the skill level required” to hack, Jung said. “Agentic tooling compresses steps that used to take a skilled operator days into hours. That is why I think defenders need to understand these tools and have detection signatures for them.”
Racem acknowledged the damage that ARTEX is causing. “The harm the [FBI] advisory describes is real, and I don’t minimize it,” they said. “The behaviour it lists (entering systems without authorization, taking data) is a crime, whoever commits it. I’m not going to pretend the tool is harmless: it automates a large part of the manual work of a penetration test, which is why it is useful, and why some people will misuse it. The authorization belongs to the operator, not to the tool.”
The reason Racem is hosting it is for small teams, they said. “I also maintain it for people testing their own systems: founders and small teams without a pentest budget can run it against their own infrastructure for the price of some API calls. I have seen people do that, and I use it myself on bug bounty programs and for AI security research,” Racem said.
Both Racem and Jung said they don’t know if the FBI advisory is talking about their specific versions of ARTEX, and really, they can’t possibly know. But, both admonished malicious use of the tool. “I take it seriously. Using ARTEX against systems without authorization is exactly what the project’s README and legal notice prohibit, and I’d encourage security teams to check their systems against the indicators of compromise the FBI published,” Jung added.
Jung said he has since added an email address people can contact if they think ARTEX was used against their systems.

About the author

Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. His work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines, shut down tech companies, and much more.

arXiv:2611.28610v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

Abstract: A policy trained against an LLM judge can learn to exploit its loopholes. Static probes show that such judges accept degenerate answers like a lone "{" or "Thought process:", but not which flaw a policy will find. In GRPO the first loophole to be exploited can be predicted before training from each pattern's exposure, the product of the starting policy's propensity to produce it and the judge's false-positive rate (FPR). To test exposure causally, we seed the patterns into fine-tuning at three doses in a Latin square. Across 36 GRPO runs with seven judges, the first exploited pattern had the highest exposure in all 12 runs with exploitation and the highest FPR in only 6. Predictions recorded before training held in three of four runs with one pattern masked by rule. When only two patterns were seeded, at 3% to 3.8% of the fine-tuning data and chosen so that exposure disagreed with FPR alone or propensity alone, exposure named the first exploited pattern and its onset window in all six runs. Exploitation occurred only on hard prompts, where an accepted exploit gets a large group-normalized advantage. Auditing exposure before RL therefore identifies the loophole a policy will likely exploit first.

Abstract: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.

# Sierra doubles valuation to $30B within six months as demand for AI in CX takes off

Ivan Mehta

6:43 AM PST · November 23, 2026

Enterprise customer experience company Sierra , co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round that doubles the company’s valuation to $30 billion. The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which valued the company at $15 billion .

The new round was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors who have led previous rounds, including Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV, and Tiger Global.

Enterprise automation is among the few areas where AI has seen rapid adoption. Sierra said that it currently serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies, and its clients include BNY, HSBC, Singtel, Wells Fargo, JPMorganChase, Pearson, Next, and Cox Automotive. The company late last month said its outcome-based pricing model has helped it double its run-rate revenue to $400 million within five months .

That said, Sierra is working along similar lines as other customer experience players in the market, which is creating a platform to build agents and partner with model developers to provide choices to enterprises. As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on creating protocol definitions for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart.

Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals.

Startups operating in the CX space have seen multimillion-dollar rounds come their way with soaring valuations. Voice AI company ElevenLabs is now valued at $22 billion; Decagon is valued at $4.5 billion ; Wonderful is valued at $5 billion ; and Parloa is valued at $3 billion . Multiple other startups have scored investments of more than $100 million.

During the HumanX conference in Amsterdam in September, Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor argued that despite the popular belief that AI-powered CX companies are replacing humans in contact centers, a majority of its customers are reassigning roles to existing employees.

results:
The FBI issued a FLASH advisory (FLASH-20261113-001, dated November 13, 2026) on ARTEX, an open-source, LLM-driven agentic hacking framework. I did not retrieve the FBI document itself, so these details come from secondary coverage.

- **Scope:** Threat actors have used the framework since at least August 2026 against finance, government, technology, defense, healthcare, and other sectors. The FBI's 13-page advisory includes indicators of compromise associated with known ARTEX campaigns, including IP addresses, command-and-control infrastructure, and suspicious network activity.
- **Campaigns:** The FBI ties ARTEX to data theft affecting about 67,000 people at South Korean financial institutions, and to a ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise that reached more than 2,250 downstream tenants (per Industrial Cyber's coverage).
- **Speed:** The FBI says some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.
- **IOC handling:** The FBI advises checking indicators against your own telemetry before blocking, because cloud addresses are reassigned. Some listed domains, such as api.anthropic.com, are common destinations, so they matter mainly when a server calls them unexpectedly alongside other suspicious activity (the FBI lists these endpoints to investigate, but they are normal destinations for many applications and are not indicators on their own).
- **Infrastructure:** Reported IOCs include Storm-3358 command-and-control and ARTEX server addresses, such as the 199.19.95.66–68 range, which the advisory's indicator table attributes to Microsoft and the FBI.
- **Detection resources:** A third-party researcher released an open-source ARTEX detection signature pack, and it warns that infrastructure indicators can go stale or produce false positives (the researcher's playbook categorizes indicators by confidence level).

Caveat: the threatdefence, aviatrix, and Latin Times pages are secondary and sometimes inconsistent in detail. Check the FBI FLASH itself, or its IC3 distribution, before operationalizing any indicator.

(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
/root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Read the end of the failed command's output. When the proxy refused or lost
   a connection while a Bash command ran, Claude Code adds [agent-proxy] lines
   there with the host and the reason. A command that ran in the background,
   or whose exit status hides the failure (piped into another command, or
   followed by "|| true"), gets none.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present,
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS points JVMs at a truststore that holds the proxy CA: the
  JDK's own store if the system trust install already added the CA there,
  otherwise /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit"). Confirm
  that JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS sets a trustStore before pointing a build at either:
  where it sets none, set-up was skipped, has not finished or has failed. If
  the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that one wins — import the
  proxy CA into it with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

Most often the destination host is not allowed for this session. Do not retry
or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the [agent-proxy] lines
give the host and, where the egress proxy answered one, the HTTP status.

### 429 / 503 from the proxy

Too many connections or requests went through the proxy, or the egress proxy
was busy. The proxy can hold a connection for about a minute before it refuses
it, so a tool with a short timeout of its own may report only a timeout. Run
fewer downloads or requests at once, then retry.

The proxy also answers 429 immediately when too many connections to it are open,
idle ones included (too_many_connections in the [agent-proxy] lines under a
failed command). Look for a program that opens connections and never closes
them. New connections work again once some have closed.

### 408 from the proxy

The tool opened a connection to the proxy and sent no complete request within 30
seconds, so the proxy closed it. Retry once. If it happens again, the tool opens
connections before it has a request to send, it is paused or short of CPU, or its
request never ends with an empty line in CRLF form (bare LF line ends, or another
protocol such as SOCKS).

### "connection reset" / "unexpected disconnect" / "RPC failed" mid-transfer

Once a tunnel is up the proxy cannot send an error response, so a connection
it aborts (tunnel to the egress proxy lost, or an upload the tunnel stopped
accepting) reaches the tool as a bare reset. The [agent-proxy] lines name the
host and reason; look for them before concluding the remote service refused the
operation.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

Some clients do not read HTTPS_PROXY: Node's built-in fetch (run that command
with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 on Node >= 22.21), aiohttp (pass trust_env=True),
Ruby bundler (reads only HTTP_PROXY, which this proxy does not serve),
hand-rolled Go dialers. Prefer the tool's own proxy option where one exists.

### git

SSH-form GitHub remotes ([email redacted]:...) are rewritten to HTTPS
automatically unless this session has its own SSH setup or supplies its own
GIT_CONFIG_*. A gitconfig that sets http.proxy / http.<url>.proxy (even empty),
its own http.sslCAInfo, or an https-to-ssh insteadOf makes git bypass the proxy
or fail verification; adjust those keys for this session if git times out.

### docker build / docker run

Processes inside containers cannot reach 127.0.0.1:37867 and do not trust
the CA. Workarounds: run builds with --network host, copy /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
into the build context and install it in an early layer, and pass proxy/CA
settings explicitly to the build.

### Not supported through the proxy (report, do not work around)

gRPC / HTTP/2-only APIs, WebSocket upgrades, client-mTLS, certificate-pinned
clients (e.g. Snowflake, ngrok), non-443 HTTPS ports, raw-TCP databases.

If a tool still cannot work through the proxy, report it so the policy or
tooling can be fixed.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender narrows attack diversity retention (ADR) earlier 0.496 relative to co-trained 0.891 at iteration twelve. Defender updates delay narrowing but dont prevent it. Successful attacks ("winners") have narrower attack diversity than the full set of generated attacks. Attacks closest to previous winners succeed 10-15 percentage points more often than those closest to previous failures. This winner-neighbor advantage holds after a defender update and for a fixed defender too. Attacks with a common opening have a common-opening advantage of 5-16 percentage points. The training row cap and update size account for little impact on ADR, and attack length accounts for only part of the ADR decrease. Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.

arXiv:2611.28660v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

arXiv:2611.28314v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

arXiv:2611.29977v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.

Abstract: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.

Abstract: Commercial AI agents increasingly incorporate long-term memory (both persistent and chat-history) to enable more accurate and personalized responses, raises significant privacy and policy concerns. Yet little is known about user privacy risks associated with memory behavior, in particular, about memory storage, disclosure, transparency and deletion control. To bridge this gap, we propose FORGETMENOT, an auditing framework for analyzing the privacy risks of long term memory in commercial AI agents. Using our framework, we collect around 3800 multi-turn sessions comprising around 6M tokens across five popular AI agents. Our results show that agents store a wide range of personal attributes, including demographics, health, and sensitive details. Furthermore, user visible memory reveals substantially less (around 20% on average) attributes than the agents store in practice, exposing a significant transparency gap. Our stealth memory injection (SMI) technique further increases the amount of personal and sensitive attribute stored in memory, raising it by 25% and 15% for Copilot and Claude, respectively. We further observed memory deletion control is unreliable, as all five agents exhibit non-zero post deletion leakage, including health and self-harm related attributes. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of memory disclosure to a 3rd-party email recipient as a proof-of-concept, as Gemini shows 31.9% leakage rate. Together, our findings reveal notable privacy risks in commercial agents memory. Finally, we discuss both design implications and regulatory recommendations to protect users memory privacy in commercial agents.

arXiv:2611.30590v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from text generation to autonomous software-engineering execution, automated vulnerability exploitability verification has emerged as a vital frontier in software quality assurance and security validation. Existing security benchmarks, however, largely judge models by binary pass/fail outcomes or coarse stage milestones. Such outcome-centric scoring obscures fine-grained failure dynamics across long-horizon execution and conflates the intrinsic capability of a base LLM with external agent scaffolding. We present POMA (Pwn-Oriented Model Assessment), a process-level evaluation methodology and platform that isolates base LLMs under a unified execution baseline -- fixing task inputs, tool interfaces, target environments, feedback formats, and execution budgets -- while measuring intermediate states and transitions from runtime evidence. Evaluating four frontier base LLMs across 55 CTF Pwn challenges and 10 real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks exposes persistent capability attrition along the exploitation chain: from vulnerability knowledge to executable implementation, from client-side actions to verified target states, from failure localization to precise repair, and across iterative revisions. In real-world software, models further struggle to satisfy format, semantic, differential, and crash-identity constraints simultaneously. By pinpointing where execution chains break down, POMA provides an empirical foundation for trustworthy capability assessment and principled vulnerability-agent design. Our benchmark catalogs, process-measurement evaluator, and sample harness are publicly available at https://github.com/maple-pwn/poma-release .

arXiv:2611.28038v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.

Abstract: Multi-criterion LLM judges often evaluate responses without specifying how conflicting criteria resolve, leaving the winner undetermined even under exact criterion scores. Issuing a strict verdict without declaring the required trade-off premise constitutes silent value completion. We introduce TradeoffBench to isolate this failure by separating rule execution from response scoring. On authoritative criterion vectors, six open-weight non-reasoning judges pass all dominance and equality controls yet pick unsupported winners on 9%-81% of 1,345 conflicts. All 577 order-stable choices follow an explicitly banned majority rule. Reasoning-enabled configurations drop anonymous-vector violations to 2 in 9,720 judgments under an explicit rule, yet cannot bridge omitted trade-offs or divergent component scoring. On raw TradeoffBench text with unspecified trade-offs, GPT-6.1-sol omits its completion premise in 29.8% of 400 verified conflicts. Even under an explicit rule on four-rater-consensus MultiPref conflicts, four reasoning judges still issue strict verdicts on 16/45 (GPT-6.1-sol) up to 35/46 and 25/29 (open-weight judges) of valid presentations. We propose identified-first evaluation, decoupling specification support, explicit completion, and target agreement. In MultiPref human-score audits, peer-mean substitution raises directional disagreement from 0.6% to 28.8% on 2,707 shared targets. A single-peer ablation confirms a 29.38-point gap on 2,175 targets, ruling out averaging as the cause. In HUMAINE, declared partial trade-offs add 2.5 percentage points of coverage, yet newly decided pairs incur 3.9% disagreement versus 0.9% for Pareto. Reliable LLM judging, therefore, requires auditing, specification support, declared trade-offs, and human target agreement separately.

- **Scope and plans:** Claude Ship is for Team and Enterprise plans, and is available on Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub.
- **Code Review (generally available):** It reviews pull requests in depth, then posts findings to the PR. It performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses, collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR.
- **PR Steward (beta):** It handles fixes but is not meant to approve. It works on failing checks, merge conflicts, and review comments from people and from review bots such as Code Review. It is designed not to approve or merge pull requests.
- **Claude Approvals (beta):** This is the approval piece. Teams write a policy file in the repository. The docs say it can set how many people have to approve changes to a path, and where Claude can post an approving review. Claude can approve routine changes under that policy, and a human can be required for sensitive ones.
- **Beta limits:** The docs say the agents aren't available to organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled, the HIPAA configuration applied, or customer-managed encryption keys. Approvals also has more limits.
- **Cost:** Claude Ship usage is billed on tokens, so turning it on can add to an organization's costs.

Sources differ slightly on the beta label. The blog and the docs' availability section call PR Steward and Approvals "beta," while the docs' product pages say "public beta."

input.prompt: What is this post, its publication date, and its main quantitative findings?

response.result:
**Publication:** "Working with AI" is an Anthropic Economics research report by Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, and Peter McCrory. It was published on November 23, 2026.

**Method:** The authors conducted 66 face-to-face interviews across 58 US companies, all Anthropic enterprise customers. The sample was selected for variety, not randomly, and the value assessments are mostly self-reported and qualitative.

**Main quantitative findings:**

- **Application coding:** Nearly 300 specific AI applications were coded by self-reported value and the degree of organizational change they required.
- **Source of value:** Most applications added value by increasing output rather than cutting costs. About half of those output gains came from accelerating existing work, and half from better quality or new products. About one-tenth of use cases benefited employees directly, through more enjoyable work or less work.
- **Software built:** Of the software interviewees described, 80% automated previously manual work and 20% replaced existing software. Figure 3 covers 140 pieces overall.
- **Hiring:** People at about two-thirds of companies reported reduced hiring due to AI. Ten companies reported hiring more, mainly for AI implementation and IT support. Only two reported AI fully eliminating a position.
- **Terminations and contractors:** Five companies described pushing out employees who wouldn't adopt AI. Nine cut contracted workers, many of whom had been offshored.
- **AI-native startups:** The six that gave estimates said they would need about four times as many employees without AI.
- **Bottlenecks:** Most cited bottlenecks came from within the organization, such as reviewing AI output and uneven adoption. Customer skepticism and regulation were rarely mentioned.

# Jensen Huang scheduled to testify next week in Senate following reinstatement as Nvidia CEO

Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to a notice on the committee’s website.

The development comes just hours after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive, less than two weeks following his resignation after it was revealed that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government of working as a Chinese spy.

The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy and his potential involvement in chip-smuggling operations.

It’s worth noting that before his reinstatement as CEO, Huang had already agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee on December 1.

# Amazon snaps up Decart’s AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips

Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.

The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.

Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video-generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.

As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post .

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”

Amazon, which has so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.

Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

- **Limits:** Shirudo currently provides an open implementation and a controlled proof of concept; automated identification, validation, and fleet-wide deployment are described as longer-term goals. Security teams should also treat shields as temporary controls, not permanent fixes.

**Title:** Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections

**Authors:** Theia Pearson-Vogel, Martin Vanek, Raymond Douglas, Jan Kulveit

**Institutions:** The page does not list author affiliations.

**Submission date:** Submitted 23 February 2026 (v1). The latest version (v3) was revised 7 November 2026.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because it exceeds the 125-character limit on quoted material. Here is a summary that keeps all the numbers:

The authors report that a Qwen 32B model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. The model denies injection in its sampled outputs, but logit lens analysis shows detection signals in the residual stream that weaken in the final layers. Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms raises sensitivity to injection from 0.3% to 39.9%, with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, which the authors argue rules out generic noise explanations. They conclude that models may have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
